lesson.title: The 3 dB Point: Why Half the Power Isn't Half the Voltage
lesson.summary: The half power point marks where delivered power falls to exactly one half of its maximum, a universal negative 3 dB marker built from average power and the decibel scale.
lesson.body:
Average power tells you how much energy per second a circuit actually delivers to a load: for a resistor carrying rms voltage V and rms current I, P equals V squared over R, which also equals I squared times R. The decibel gives engineers a compact, multiplicative way to compare two power levels on a logarithmic scale, using dB equals 10 log10 of the power ratio. The half power point sits at the intersection of these two ideas: it is the specific point, almost always a frequency, at which the power delivered to a load has fallen to exactly one half of some reference power, typically the maximum power the circuit is capable of delivering.

Because power depends on the square of voltage or current, a drop to half power does not mean a drop to half voltage. It means a drop to 1 over the square root of 2, approximately 0.7071, since squaring that number gives 0.5. This trips up a lot of students the first time they see it: half the power corresponds to about seventy one percent of the voltage or current amplitude, not fifty percent.

Expressed in decibels, the half power point always comes out to the same number whether you compute it from power or from amplitude. From power: 10 log10(0.5) equals negative 3.01 dB. From amplitude: 20 log10(0.7071) also equals negative 3.01 dB. Both paths land on the same value because squaring a ratio inside a logarithm doubles the logarithm, and the decibel formula compensates by using 20 instead of 10 for amplitude ratios. That is why this point is universally called the 3 dB point, or described as a signal being 3 dB down, whether the person saying it is thinking in power or in voltage.

Here is a fully worked check. Suppose a circuit's output voltage at its strongest frequency is 10 V rms across a purely resistive 50 ohm load. Maximum power is P_max equals 10 squared over 50, which is 100 over 50, or 2 W. Half of that is 1 W. Solving for the voltage that produces 1 W across 50 ohms: V equals the square root of P times R, which is the square root of 1 times 50, or the square root of 50, which equals 7.0711 V. Check the ratio: 7.0711 divided by 10 equals 0.70711, matching 1 over the square root of 2 exactly as predicted. In decibels, 20 log10(0.70711) equals negative 3.01 dB, confirming that the power at this voltage really has been cut in half.

This single fixed marker is what makes filter design a shared language rather than a matter of opinion. Without an agreed rule for where a response has meaningfully rolled off, every engineer could draw the edge of a passband somewhere different. With the half power point pinned down, that edge is always the same, and it is exactly the boundary the next chapter uses to define cutoff frequency.
